canberra.title: Brumby advocate loses urgent bid to halt Kosciuszko cull
canberra.snippet: The NSW Land and Environment Court has rejected a second urgent attempt this year to halt wild horse culling operations in Kosciuszko Nat...
canberra.content:
The NSW Land and Environment Court has rejected a second urgent bid this year to halt wild horse culling in Kosciuszko National Park. Photo: NSW Courts.

The NSW Land and Environment Court has rejected a second urgent attempt this year to halt wild horse culling operations in Kosciuszko National Park (KNP).

Brumby advocate Carmen Jackson filed for an injunction on Thursday (27 August), seeking to prevent aerial and ground shooting, trapping, removal and killing in trap yards while the court considered her broader legal challenge.

At the centre of her case is whether the department and those carrying out the operations have the authority required to trap, shoot or otherwise harm wild horses in the park.

Ms Jackson represented herself when the application came before Justice Sarah Pritchard the following Wednesday (2 September).

Justice Pritchard dismissed the injunction after finding Ms Jackson had not established a serious question over whether the staff involved were properly authorised.

Ms Jackson questioned whether each employee, contractor, shooter and trap operator involved had the authority required under the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1974.

The act generally prohibits people from harming animals in national parks unless they are authorised to do so or are carrying out a legal duty.

Ms Jackson did not claim the required authorisations did not exist, but said she had been unable to identify them.

Instead, she wanted the NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW) to identify the authorisations being relied on, including who issued them, when they were made and which people, animals, locations and control methods they covered.

She argued the operations should be suspended until the case was decided because any harm caused in the meantime would be irreversible.

“Once an individual horse has been killed, that consequence cannot be reversed by a subsequent judgment of the court,” Ms Jackson said in an affidavit.

DCCEEW argued the operations were authorised under the Kosciuszko National Park Wild Horse Heritage Management Plan 2021 (WHHMP) and the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1974 (NPW Act), which requires the department’s secretary to put the plan into effect.

Under the WHHMP, approved control methods include passive trapping, mustering, removal for rehoming or transport to an abattoir or knackery, shooting in trap yards, ground shooting and aerial shooting.

DCCEEW principal legal officer Nicholas Sandstrom told the court all 10 National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) employees involved in operations before the aerial shoot scheduled to begin on 2 November had authorisations under section 171 of the NPW Act.

Six were covered by a general authorisation issued in December 2019, while four held individual authorisations.

Justice Pritchard accepted the evidence that the staff were legally permitted to harm animals in a national park.

The court then considered whether the consequences of stopping the operations outweighed the harm that would result from allowing them to continue.

Ms Jackson argued there was a, “fundamental asymmetry” between temporarily postponing operations and killing horses, which could not be reversed.

DCCEEW argued a delay would disrupt planned operations, increase costs and allow environmental damage caused by wild horses to continue.

The court heard postponing the November aerial operation could require NPWS to redeploy 14 staff, including four trained shooters.

If its helicopters were unavailable when the operation was rescheduled, replacements would cost around $12,925 a day to hire, they said.

Under the WHHMP, the wild horse population must be reduced to 3000 in designated retention areas by 30 June 2027 and maintained at zero elsewhere in the park.

The court heard the population in surveyed areas was estimated at 10,309 in October 2025.

DCCEEW said wild horses damaged native habitat through grazing, trampling and erosion, and degraded streams and wetlands.

The WHHMP also records damage to Aboriginal artefacts and cultural landscapes.

Justice Pritchard accepted that killing horses caused irreversible harm and acknowledged the strong feelings held by Ms Jackson and other members of the community.

However, she found stopping the operations would have consequences beyond financial and administrative disruption, including allowing environmental damage to continue and making it harder to meet the required population target.

She found the, “balance of convenience” favoured allowing the operations to continue.

The decision is the latest in a series of legal challenges to wild horse control operations in NSW.

In July, Matthew Holland and Roxanne Phoenix unsuccessfully sought an injunction against aerial and ground shooting in KNP after dead horses, including pregnant mares and what appeared to be an aborted foal, were found near Kiandra.

They argued the operations were cruel and breached animal welfare laws and the park’s management plan.

Justice John Robson found the evidence was insufficient to raise a serious question to be tried.

Their broader case is listed for a final hearing on 22 and 23 October.

Ms Jackson has also challenged shooting and trapping operations in Yuraygir National Park on the NSW North Coast.

Justice Rachel Pepper refused her application for an urgent injunction on 25 August, finding there was insufficient evidence to raise a serious question over whether the cull was lawfully authorised.

DCCEEW nevertheless agreed to suspend operations until the case’s final hearing on 9 and 10 September.

Meanwhile, ground shooting continued in KNP until Friday (4 September), while passive trapping and removal were also underway when approved rehomers were available.

No aerial shooting is scheduled until 2 November.

Ms Jackson’s broader Kosciuszko challenge remains before the court and will be heard on 1 October.

Original Article published by Edwina Mason on About Regional.

canberra.title: Nurse jailed for indecently abusing elderly patient at aged care home
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual abuse. When an elderly resident at a Canberra aged care home asked for a massage, the only...
canberra.content:
Anslem Uzochukwu Uponi, 34, has been jailed over the abuse he inflicted on a patient. Photo: Albert McKnight.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual abuse.

When an elderly resident at a Canberra aged care home asked for a massage, the only nurse on shift that night instead violently broke the trust he owed her as the person responsible for her care.

Former registered nurse Anslem Uzochukwu Uponi has been handed a jail sentence for indecently assaulting his vulnerable female patient, who was in her mid-70s, at the facility in November 2024.

The 34-year-old did not visibly react when Corrective officers took him into custody after he was sentenced by the ACT Magistrates Court on Thursday (3 September).

The court heard that he had been the only registered nurse working on a night shift at the facility, which meant he was in a position of trust.

Magistrate Alexandra Burt said the patient had asked him for a massage for therapeutic purposes, but the massage “transgressed those boundaries”.

She found that Uponi started indecently touching the patient’s body during the massage. The patient asked him to get off her, but he didn’t, and she had to move her body and use her weight to force him off her.

Uponi pleaded not guilty and fought the allegations at a hearing. But Magistrate Burt was satisfied the offending did occur and found him guilty of a charge of committing an act of indecency without consent.

The magistrate said there had been a question over whether the assault was motivated by his sexual gratification. Ultimately, she found that it was, as he climbed on top of the patient, he started rocking back and forth, then didn’t stop when she asked him to.

Uponi’s lawyer, Legal Aid’s Ewan Small, fought for his client to receive an intensive corrections order (ICO), which is a community-based sentence of imprisonment.

“There’s nothing to suggest that he would be getting away with an easy outcome,” he said.

Mr Small said his client had no prior criminal history, was a relatively young man with a family and noted the massage had started out consensual before his client overstepped the boundaries.

But prosecutor Liam Taylor said there was a need for adequate punishment, protection of the community, and to denounce the conduct of the offender. A full-time jail sentence was appropriate, he argued.

The court heard that Uponi was born in Nigeria, had lived in Australia for the last 10 years, and was now surviving on Centrelink payments as he was no longer allowed to work as a nurse.

His nursing registration had been suspended due to his charge. Magistrate Burt said this was a natural consequence of his offending, but she took it into account as a form of extra-curial punishment.

“Ultimately, this is a matter, in my view, that calls strongly for general deterrence,” she said.

“It is of concern trained nurses … adhere to professional standards and do not act in a manner that is indecent when at work.”

Uponi was sentenced to six months’ jail, with the remainder suspended until October 2026, after he spent one month behind bars. He must then complete an 18-month good behaviour order.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on (02) 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on (02) 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on (02) 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call triple zero.

You can also submit an online report about a historical sexual assault allegation for incidents that occurred more than six months ago.

canberra.title: Master Builders ACT wins major accolades at regional Training Awards
canberra.snippet: Master Builders ACT took home two major awards at this year’s ACT Training Awards, winning both Small Training Provider of the Year...
canberra.content:
4 September 2026

Start the conversation

MBA Training Carpentry graduate Emmi Lee took home the ACT Apprentice of the Year award. Photo: Thomas Lucraft.

Master Builders ACT took home two major awards at this year’s ACT Training Awards, winning both Small Training Provider of the Year and ACT Apprentice of the Year.

Held at the National Convention Centre on 3 September, the annual ACT Training Awards showcase the outstanding achievements of the ACT’s vocational education and training (VET) sector across the territory, recognising the individuals and organisations driving skills development and workforce growth.

Winning Small Training Provider of the Year for their delivery of high-quality construction training in the region, Master Builders ACT CEO Anna Neelagama said the award highlights the organisation’s commitment to delivering modern, accredited courses that prepare the ACT’s next generation to exceed standard vocational benchmarks.

“Championing quality in the ACT building and construction industry is at the heart of everything we do at MBA Training,” Ms Neelagama said.

“This award is a huge recognition of the efforts of our hardworking trainers and administrative team, who are among the best in the industry.

“They bring extensive industry experience and genuine passion to every classroom and worksite to ensure our trainees not only meet industry standards, but exceed them.

“This win is about building a better building industry for the ACT and region. With all 26 construction trades currently in shortage in the ACT, growing the future construction workforce has never been more critical.

“The students who walk through our doors today are our future builders, civil construction engineers, project managers and safety experts. They are the future of our building industry, and we are proud to play a role in shaping it.”

Recent MBA Training carpentry graduate Emmi Lee was honoured with the title of ACT Apprentice of the Year.

“Emmi’s achievement sends a powerful message: there is a place for women in every corner of the construction industry,” Ms Neelagama said.

“At Master Builders ACT, we are proud to champion women in construction. We want to see our female apprentices thriving at the highest level. Emmi represents the best of what our training programs can deliver, and I have no doubt she will be a leader in the industry in the years to come.”

MBA Training, along with other aligned winners, will represent the ACT at the Australian Training Awards, to be held at the International Convention Centre in Sydney on 20 November.

canberra.title: ‘Heartbroken doesn’t cover it’: Family remembers cyclist killed in double-fatal crash
canberra.snippet: Bridie Lee was her younger sister’s best-friend from almost the moment she was born. The pair came from a very tight family, but we...
canberra.content:
Bridie Lee was deeply loved by her family and more: (clockwise from top left), Bridie, Bridie with her brother David and sister Amy, and Bridie with her best-friend/housemate Alice and Alice’s dog Squirrel. Photos: Supplied by family.

Bridie Lee was her younger sister’s best-friend from almost the moment she was born.

The pair came from a very tight family, but were different while growing up in Western Australia. Amy Lee, two years younger, remembers being shy, while Bridie was the one who would confidently strike up a conversation with anybody.

“She taught me to be brave,” Amy said.

“She always had me under her wing and was always looking after me.

“I think if I didn’t have her protection and didn’t have her looking after me, then I wouldn’t have come out of my shell.”

Their close relationship continued through the years even though they lived on opposite sides of the world – Bridie moved to work in Canberra in 2022 while Amy relocated to the United Kingdom.

Due to the time difference between continents, the sisters would leave each other voice message recordings to keep in contact. Bridie would always finish off her messages by telling her sister how much she loved her and how proud she was of her.

“I’m really glad we did that now, because I’ve got all these recordings of her voice,” Amy told Region in an emotional call this week.

Bridie and four other cyclists were riding on Gungahlin Drive in northern Canberra after 6 am on 27 August 2026 when a car crashed into their group.

The 32-year-old died at the scene from her injuries. Two male cyclists were taken to hospital and while a 34-year-old man was soon released, the tragedy continued when a 39-year-old man died in hospital seven days later.

On Friday (4 September), an ACT Policing spokesperson said the investigation into the double-fatal crash was continuing and the 40-year-old female driver of the car was assisting police with their inquiries.

All of the cyclists had been riding as part of the Canberra Bilbys Triathlon Club’s regular cycling group.

The impact of Bridie’s death has reverberated around the ACT community, where she was a popular colleague at the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) and a beloved member of the triathlon club. But back in Western Australia is her grieving family, suffering a loss beyond words.

“It’s hard seeing Mum and Dad. ‘Heartbroken’ doesn’t even cover it,” Amy said.

“I feel awful myself, but it’s even more awful to see my family in such pain.

“But genuinely, we find it really, really comforting to hear from so many people, telling us such lovely stories about her.”

Bridie Lee (centre) with her parents John and Carolyn at her graduation from Curtin University. Photo: Supplied by family.

Amy said the number one thing to know about her sister was that she was really funny.

“Ever since she was little, she was always cracking jokes, making bad puns and trying to make others around her laugh,” she said.

Bridie was always so open and friendly, and would chat to everybody.

“I was always jealous of how she made friends so easily. It was just natural for her, she was someone who people were drawn to,” Amy said.

She finished her Honours in biomedical sciences and her Masters in epidemiology and statistics, which helped satisfy her love of learning. She had an incredible amount of knowledge about many subjects.

“She was the sort of person who would just sit down and watch random documentaries about random stuff,” Amy said.

Bridie moved away from everyone she knew to join a graduate program at the ABS in Canberra. But she stayed at the bureau once she finished, as she loved her work.

“I’m so proud that she was always so kind, not only to other people, but to animals,” Amy said.

“She was known around the ABS as the person who would rescue little hurt birds on the side of the road.”

She was also always busy, always trying new activities. She practiced archery, become involved with gridiron and found a passion for triathlons.

“Anything she wanted to do, she would go out and try it,” Amy said.

“I don’t think she would have any regrets, because she was somebody who appreciated life and lived life to the fullest.”

Sisters Bridie and Amy Lee (left), as well as pictured at a Matildas match with Bridie’s best-friend and housemate Alice. Photos: Supplied by family.

Region asked Amy how her family wanted the community to remember her sister.

“We just want her to be remembered how everybody remembered her, as a really kind, beautiful soul, and as the jokester who wanted to make everybody laugh,” she said.

Seeing as Bridie was such a jokester, what was her favourite joke?

A really bad one she would tell all the time, Amy laughed.

“What do you call a cheese that isn’t yours? Nacho cheese,” Bridie would say.

canberra.title: A brilliant exhibition of David Hockney’s images of people at the NGA
canberra.snippet: The ranking of artists is not the prerogative of contemporaries – it is the role of posterity. David Hockney died on 11 June 2026 and we ...
canberra.content:
4 September 2026

Start the conversation

David Hockney, Celia in a black dress with red stockings, 1973, National Gallery of Australia, Kamberri/Canberra, gift of Orde Poynton Esq CMG 1998. © Estate of David Hockney Photo: NGA.

The ranking of artists is not the prerogative of contemporaries – it is the role of posterity. David Hockney died on 11 June 2026 and we are scrambling to ascertain and comprehend his legacy.

He was unbelievably prolific and impossible to pin down. He was a key contributor to the pop art movement of the 1960s with paintings, prints and collages.

Hockney was an outstanding stage set designer, employing his neurological condition of synaesthesia, through which his associations of sound, colour and shape led to the most unusual, visually vibrant opera stage sets.

He was also an obsessive photographer and contributor to the various digital arts, especially in depicting people and landscapes.

Hockney was an incredibly curious artist, endlessly fascinated by how we see things and how that can be manipulated in art. However, more than anything, he was preoccupied with the human figure, portraiture and commentary on the human condition.

Much of Hockney’s art was autobiographical and, as a gay man, he fled the restrictions of his native Britain to the relative freedom of Los Angeles and in his art celebrated those whom he loved, frequently depicted with homoerotic detail.

Hockney could draw like an angel with a line that not only articulated form but introduced a touch of sensuousness.

David Hockney (artist), Tyler Graphics (printer and publisher), Red Celia, 1984, National Gallery of Australia, Kamberri/Canberra, purchased 1986. © Estate of David Hockney/Tyler Graphics Ltd Photo: NGA.

The National Gallery of Australia holds more than 1000 works by Hockney, with over 60 on display in this exhibition.

The earliest pieces date from 1961 and the most recent from 2012 – it is a spectacular half century of Hockney treasures.

There are drawings, etchings, lithographs, paper pulp prints, photographs, fax art, photocopy art and a few animated iPad pieces on loan from the David Hockney Studio.

A number of the pieces could be described as iconic Hockney works that have featured in many Hockney retrospective exhibitions; others are rare or unique and stem from the Ken Tyler archive or judicious purchases.

The crayon drawing, Celia in a black dress with red stockings, 1973, is a miracle of drawing, once you get to know it.

Celia Birtwell was a British textile and fashion designer and one of Hockney’s closest friends whom he drew constantly over several decades.

This drawing looks casual and yet conveys a remarkable amount of information. More than a decade later, Hockney’s Red Celia, 1984, lithograph reinterprets her features to create this icon in British art.

David Hockney (artist), Atelier Crommelynck (printer), Propyläen Verlag (publisher), The student: homage to Picasso, 1973, National Gallery of Australia, Kamberri/Canberra, purchased 1980. © Estate of David Hockney Photo: NGA.

Another iconic image is Hockney’s etching The student: homage to Picasso, 1973, where he presents himself in a Panama hat and wearing his signature round glasses as he approaches a bust of the young Picasso on the plinth – a work made in the year of Picasso’s death.

Hockney’s printer, Aldo Crommelynck, was also Picasso’s master printer and in a way Hockney is hinting at a homage to the master while following in his footsteps.

David Hockney, Gregory in the pool, paper pool 4, 1978, National Gallery of Australia, Kamberri/Canberra, purchased 1979. © Estate of David Hockney Photo: NGA.

The exhibition includes numerous images of Hockney’s lovers, including the image of Gregory in the pool, 1978, printed by his friend and long-term collaborator, Ken Tyler, using his unique coloured paper pulp technique.

Gregory Evans reappears six years later in Tyler’s collaged colour lithograph, An image of Gregory, 1984-85, from the artist’s Moving focus series.

David Hockney (artist), Tyler Graphics (printer and publisher), An image of Gregory, 1984-85, National Gallery of Australia, Kamberri/Canberra, gift of Kenneth Tyler 2002. © Estate of David Hockney/Tyler Graphics Ltd Photo: NGA.

The earliest pieces in the exhibition are etchings from Hockney’s A rake’s progress series from 1961 to 1963, with the unforgettable image of the artist dyeing his hair blonde on his first journey to New York and creating his trademark appearance, the latest are the iPad pieces from 2012.

Throughout, Hockney interrogates the human face with amazing skill, wit and introspection.

Hockney once said: “The eye is always moving; if it isn’t moving you are dead.”

What particularly struck me about this superb exhibition, beautifully curated by Magda Keaney, is the artist’s lively intellect, exceptional skill level and his ability to make the human form, especially the face, into something that is in constant motion, telling us a fascinating story with passion and infectious enthusiasm.

David Hockney: Portraits in Print, is at the National Gallery of Australia, gallery 13, from 5 September to 9 May 2027, free entry.

australia.title: Pocock says skilled migrants should be top priority as Australia faces shortage of AI workers and tradies – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast ‘Gut-wrenching’: Bowen to meet with Nepali community...
australia.content:
Albanese extends condolences to Nepal PM

The prime minister said he has spoken with Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, to “extend Australia’s deepest condolences” after the deadly flash floods.

In a post on social media, Albanese said Australia “stands by Nepal” and is continuing to provide humanitarian aid “where it’s needed most”.

The loss of life and destruction is devastating, and we will keep doing everything we can to find the Australians still unaccounted for.

Our thoughts are with the families and loved ones of those Australians who are still missing.

The government said 36 Australians remain missing after two more people were safely located on Friday.

    Welcome

What we learned today, Friday 4 September

That’s where we’ll leave our live coverage for today.

Before we go, let’s recap the day’s top headlines:

  • The new ACTU secretary, Melissa Donnelly, said cost-of-living issues and the rollout of AI in workplaces are two major focuses of her new role.

  • Two more Australians have been confirmed safe in the aftermath of the devastating Nepal-Tibet floods. The prime minister said he has extended Australia’s “deepest condolences” to Nepal’s PM.

  • Chris Bowen has called a joint statement about China’s missile test “strong” despite it not referring to the nation by name.

  • Sydney has its first confirmed case of H5 bird flu after a greater crested tern found on the northern beaches tested positive for the virus.

  • Tanya Plibersek said the government was considering other ways it could help protect young people from online harms, including pornography, during a roundtable today.

  • Molly Ticehurst’s killer Daniel Billings called a woman he had met on Tinder and confessed to his crime, a court heard today.

  • The masterminds behind a major corruption scheme over cleaning contracts for a state rail network have been jailed over their “corrosive” offending.

  • Five people have been hospitalised after a forklift fire at a commercial site in Brisbane. Two women were taken to hospital in life-threatening conditions and three men were transported for smoke inhalation.

  • A total fire ban will be in place for the greater Sydney region after authorities issued an extreme fire danger forecast for Saturday 5 September.

Thanks for sticking around, have a lovely weekend!

Pocock says skilled migrants should be ‘No 1 priority’ as AI boom and housing sector face staff shortages

Senator David Pocock says skilled migrants should be the “No 1 priority” as new data shows Australia is falling short of the workers needed to power both the nation’s AI boom and housing targets.

This week, the Powering Skills Organisation, a government-established jobs and skills body, warned that Australia needs 72,000 more electricians and related tradespeople by 2030 to meet project demand.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Pocock said:

I don’t understand why Jobs and Skills Australia doesn’t have them as the No 1 priority. When we look at the migration figures, how can we have a shortage of something so critical as tradies to build the houses we desperately need?

This is one of my huge frustrations about this immigration debate and the population debate. We have both sides of politics arguing over the number, how big it should be, what it shouldn’t be … we have no plan. Surely, that’s the starting point.

Pocock warns Australia risks US-style AI datacentre backlash without long-term return

Independent senator David Pocock has warned Australia risks facing similar social licence issues over AI datacentres as the United States unless it puts in place “some sort of mechanism to get a long-term return”.

The comments come after the federal defence minister, Richard Marles, and industry and innovation minister, Andrew Charlton, met with major US AI companies during a trip to meet their American counterparts.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Pocock said:

In the US they are facing massive issues when it comes to social licence.

I’m still concerned the government isn’t answering the bigger question: what’s the long-term benefit of hosting these datacentres here? It seems to me these big multinational tech companies are expert at minimising their taxable income here in Australia, paying very little tax, and yet we’ll be hosting this supposedly gamechanging infrastructure.

So, I don’t understand why we aren’t putting in place some sort of mechanism to get a long-term return.

Time running out to keep housing developer afloat

A deadline to secure funding to keep embattled housing developer Bathla Group afloat has been pushed out to Monday as creditors absorb a breakdown of the group’s $3.4bn debt, AAP reports.

Insolvency advisory Teneo has been scrambling to secure short-term funding for Bathla since it entered voluntary administration in late August.

A creditors’ meeting on Friday was presented details of the company’s debt picture.

Teneo will continue negotiations with lenders over the weekend to try to secure funding before a staff meeting on Monday to inform Bathla employees if a short-term package has been agreed.

Money to cover payroll had been secured through refunds of bonds held by entities such as Sydney Water, a source close to the negotiations told AAP on Friday.

“It’s a very volatile situation because there’s no money and time is running out,” said the source, who asked not to be named for commercial privacy reasons.

The worst-case scenario if no funding came through was for building operations to shut down, they said.

Figures presented to creditors showed Bathla’s total debt at $3.4bn, including $3.08bn to secured lenders, $130m to unsecured lenders, $145m to the tax office and $4m to employees.

Read more:

Cyclist Rohan Dennis seeks new judge for driving breach

Former Olympic cyclist Rohan Dennis has faced court after pleading guilty to driving while suspended, appearing before the same judge who warned him he would be jailed if he breached the ban, AAP reports.

Lawyers for Dennis, 36, told the Adelaide district court on Friday that they intended to lodge an application seeking the recusal of Judge Ian Press from hearing the case.

Dennis was given a suspended 17-month jail term and banned from driving for five years in 2025 after pleading guilty to a charge over the events leading up to the death of his Olympian wife, Melissa Hoskins.

Hoskins, 32, was struck by her husband’s vehicle near their home at Medindie, in Adelaide’s inner north, on 30 December 2023.

He intended to apply for a recusal of Press, Dennis’s lawyer Craig Caldicott said.

Outside court, Caldicott declined to say whether the recusal application was connected to Press’s assertion that Dennis would be jailed for driving while disqualified.

“It’s appropriate in the circumstances to seek a recusal in this matter,” he said.

Asked what was wrong with this judge, he said:

There’s nothing wrong with this judge, he’s a very good judge.

He accepted Dennis could go to jail. He said:

There’s always a possibility on any matter, you should be well aware that driving while disqualified, he could go to jail.

Total fire ban issued for greater Sydney region on Saturday

A total fire ban will be in place for the greater Sydney region after authorities issued an extreme fire danger forecast for Saturday 5 September.

Elevated fire dangers come as the Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) forecast unseasonably warm conditions and a potential top of 31C.

The BoM has also issued a severe weather warning for Saturday and anticipates strong winds for large parts of the state.

NSW rural fire services have urged residents to “take action now. Know your fire risk and what you will do if fire threatens.”

Albanese extends condolences to Nepal PM

The prime minister said he has spoken with Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, to “extend Australia’s deepest condolences” after the deadly flash floods.

In a post on social media, Albanese said Australia “stands by Nepal” and is continuing to provide humanitarian aid “where it’s needed most”.

The loss of life and destruction is devastating, and we will keep doing everything we can to find the Australians still unaccounted for.

Our thoughts are with the families and loved ones of those Australians who are still missing.

The government said 36 Australians remain missing after two more people were safely located on Friday.

Read more:

Five people hospitalised after forklift fire in Brisbane

Five people have been hospitalised after a forklift fire at a commercial site in Brisbane.

Emergency services responded to reports of a fire just before 11am this morning on Anton Road in Hemmant.

Seven trucks were deployed to the scene where fire fighters battled a blaze that had spread to neighbouring containers in the immediate area. The fire was extinguished at 2.15pm.

An official with Queensland’s fire service told reporters earlier:

An industrial forklift contains a lot of lubricants … and oils.

The containers that were on fire were refrigerated shipping containers so they are insulated with insulation foam. That would have attributed to a lot of the smoke we saw.

Queensland Ambulance Service said two women were taken to hospital in life-threatening conditions and three men were transported for smoke inhalation.

Nick Visser

That’s all for me. Achol Arok will guide you into the weekend. Take care.

Benita Kolovos

Victoria’s premier says public official found to have engaged in ‘serious and concerning conduct’ no longer serving in his role

The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, has confirmed that a public servant who was found last month to have engaged in “serious and concerning conduct” after a corruption investigation has left his role.

Carroll told reporters earlier today that Tony Bates was no longer secretary of the Department of Education and would be leaving the public service. A search for his replacement is under way.

Bates took a leave of absence after an investigation by the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (Ibac), released last month, found he was part of a group of government officials who engaged in “serious and concerning” conduct while negotiating firefighter pay deals with Peter Marshall – the secretary of the United Firefighters Union (UFU).

The inquiry found Bates was involved in the negotiations, which occurred without the knowledge of the emergency services minister.

On Friday, Carroll said:

I read the Ibac Operation Richmond back to front, and I made it very clear that integrity is non-negotiable and a deal essentially was done behind a minister’s back.

Bates is the third public servant head to depart since Carroll took over from Jacinta Allan in late July. The head of the Department of Premier and Cabinet, Jeremi Moule was replaced by Treasury secretary, Chris Barrett, days after Carroll became premier and last week transport head Jeroen Weimar announced he would also leave his position.

More on the Ibac report here:

Ima Caldwell

Second cyclist dies following Canberra crash

A second person has died after a crash in Canberra’s north last week, ACT police confirmed.

The 39-year-old man died in hospital yesterday evening, one week after a car ploughed into a group of five cyclists on Gungahlin Drive in Palmerston, between Wells Station Drive and Kosciusko Ave.

A 32-year-old female rider died at the scene, while a 39-year-old man was taken to the hospital in critical condition.

Police confirmed his death this morning, increasing the number of deaths on ACT roads this year to 11.

Ex-rail boss in Victoria jailed over corrupt contracts

The masterminds behind a major corruption scheme over cleaning contracts for a state rail network have been jailed over their “corrosive” offending, AAP reports.

Former V/Line chief executive James Pinder was jailed for two years and eight months with a non-parole period of one year and nine months for misconduct of public office in the Victorian county court on Thursday.

Transclean co-director George Haritos was handed a term of two years and three months with a minimum of one year and five months for conspiracy to give a secret commission and two counts of giving secret commissions.

The company’s other co-director Alex Kyritsis and employees Steven Kyritsis and Maria Tsakopoulos were each given community corrections orders and ordered to do unpaid community service.

All five pleaded guilty to charges brought by the Victorian corruption watchdog following its Operation Esperance investigation into serious corrupt conduct in the state’s V/Line and Metro’s tendering and procurement processes.

The offending occurred between April 2018 to August 2020, when Pinder, as V/Line boss, participated in awarding a large-scale cleaning contract to Transclean worth more than $54m.

Andrew Messenger

Queensland ambulance bug in triple-zero system resolved

A computer bug which forced the Queensland ambulance service to use a backup dispatch system to answer triple-zero calls has been resolved.

The service switched on a new computer aided dispatch system on Wednesday. The Guardian understands users had latency issues – computer lag – on Thursday, forcing the ambulance service to use a planned manual backup.

That meant some calls were completed over the radio with information entered manually, rather than using a computer aided dispatch system.

The problem has been resolved and the new computer aided system turned back on.

A spokesperson for the Queensland ambulance service said “all triple-zero calls are being answered and resources are being dispatched in a timely manner, with the most urgent cases prioritised”.

The Guardian understands that the service believes no high-priority patient was delayed treatment, though some less urgent cases may have had delays. The ambulance service has a service staffed by paramedics, doctors, nurses and allied health professionals which keeps in touch with low-triage patients waiting for an ambulance.

“As is best practice, business continuity processes were enacted during the transition to the new CAD system to maintain operational oversight and call-taking and dispatch services,” the spokesperson said.

There was no impact to triple-zero calls to the QAS while business continuity processes were in place. Any reporting to the contrary is false.

Molly Ticehurst’s killer called woman he had met on Tinder after stabbing, court hears

Two hours after Daniel Billings murdered his ex-girlfriend Molly Ticehurst in a frenzied stabbing he spoke to a woman he had met on Tinder, AAP reports.

“I’m sorry I murdered her,” Billings told the woman during a phone call at 2.02am on 22 April 2024.

The woman, who Billings met on the dating app in early 2022, told police she was shocked as he described the murder during their brief conversation.

He made the phone call from a mutual friend’s property, where Billings had fled in his bloodied clothes, according to a statement of facts.

The friend soon alerted police, the court heard.

Read more here:

Andrew Messenger

Former Queensland police commissioner Steve Gollschewski dies

The former Queensland police commissioner Steve Gollschewski has died from cancer.

The 46-year veteran retired from the QPS in February. He was the state’s longest-serving cop.

He was appointed commissioner in 2024, before being diagnosed with cancer in 2025 and stepping down. He briefly returned to the force six months later.

Acting commissioner Brett Pointing said Gollschewski “will be remembered as an exceptional leader who used insight and innovation to strengthen the organisation and help keep the community safe”.

“Throughout his distinguished career, Steve was a remarkable strategist and contemporary leader, disciplined in his thinking, measured in his decisions and guided by deeply held personal values,” Pointing said.

The police minister, Dan Purdie, said Gollschewski wass the third-longest serving officer in the history of the service.

“My thoughts are with the loved ones of former Police Commissioner Steve Gollschewski AO APM following the news of his tragic passing,” he said.

The Queensland premier, David Crisafulli, said Gollschewski had “devoted his life to the Queensland Police Service, upholding our laws and making our state a safer place”.

Big tech ‘making money’ from harming children, Plibersek says

Tanya Plibersek, the federal minister for social services, spoke a few moments ago about the additional ways Australia needs to strengthen the regulation potential for algorithms.

She said:

People should be able to opt out of getting violent and degrading stuff online. We know that an account set up by a teenage boy takes an average of 23 minutes to be fed misogynistic content online. That is a deliberate decision of Big Tech to do that.

They are making money out of harming our children. We need to look at what additional powers we need to deal with that.

Petra Stock

Victoria records state’s first H5 bird flu cases in mammals

Victoria has recorded its first cases of deadly H5 bird flu in mammals, including a confirmed case in red fox at Torquay, and a suspected positive case in a dolphin at Lorne, the state’s acting chief veterinary officer, Dr Cameron Bell, said.

Since 20 June, the state has confirmed 212 positive cases from 892 investigations.

The chief biodiversity officer, James Todd, said heading into the spring breeding season surveillance efforts would be focused on high-risk areas, including the Mornington Peninsula, Port Phillip Bay, Western Port Bay and the Gippsland lakes, places that were important breeding grounds for waterbirds and marine mammals and near poultry facilities. He said further mortality events and spread into other species was expected. He said:

We’re at the beginning of a virus, which will continue to impact on Victoria’s wildlife.

We know that people care deeply about wildlife, and the impacts that the community may be observing, in terms of dying and dead wildlife, is really confronting and distressing.

Tory Shepherd

A renowned forensic scientist on Nepal’s ‘extreme challenges’

The bodies of some of those killed in the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster may never be found, and some of those that are may never be identified, a world-renowned forensic scientist says.

Prof Richard Bassed, the head of forensic medicine at Melbourne’s Monash University, spent three months in Thailand after the 2004 Boxing Day tsunami and also helped to identify victims of Victoria’s catastrophic Black Saturday bushfires in 2009.

Now he has watched as authorities in Nepal and Tibet struggle to find and identify the dead amid the agonies of the living after last week’s devastating flash flood. More than 1,250 people have been confirmed dead, with more than 5,000 missing.

Read more here:

australia.title: Afternoon Update: EV sales outpace petrol cars; workers found alive in Nepal; and illiterate boyfriend tests
australia.snippet: Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Afternoon Update here , and start your day with our Morning Mail newsletter...
australia.content:
Good afternoon.

Electric vehicle sales in Australia have exceeded petrol cars for the first time.

More than 27,000 EVs were sold in August, a new record for a single month and representing 24.9% of new cars sold. The climate-friendly technology surpassed both petrol vehicles (nearly 26,000 sold) and diesel cars (23,600).

The rise in EVs has been helped by two factors – the war in Iran pushing up oil prices and making running a petrol car significantly more expensive, and the introduction last year of a federal vehicle emissions standard that required auto companies to cut average tailpipe emissions year-on-year.

The climate change and energy minister, Chris Bowen, said EV sales surpassing petrol cars was a “landmark moment”.

---

A note before leaving you with the rest of the news. This email is changing. From Monday you’ll be receiving our new-look newsletter Politics, really, as explained in the blue box we’ve been including in this email each day this week.

Helmed by our political editor, Tom McIlroy, and our team of political reporters in Canberra, Politics, really will be in your inbox at 5pm AEST every weekday and will continue to bring you the best news, the best podcasts, features, and puzzles you have come to love.

Top news

  • Nepal-Tibet flash flood: Two workers pulled alive from hydropower tunnel nine days after disaster

  • Shaky foundations: Bathla’s downfall is one of many warning signs for Australia’s construction industry

  • Molly Ticehurst’s killer called woman he’d met on Tinder after stabbing and said ‘I’m sorry I murdered her’, court hears

  • Pedicures and a pair of socks: sailors from USS Abraham Lincoln go wild in party resort of Pattaya

  • New Zealand drugs regulator approves use of MDMA to treat severe PTSD

In pictures

The UN general assembly will vote on Friday on a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe (introduced by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate the seas) in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size.

Historians and geographers have said for years that the Mercator projection is rooted in western stereotypes. Activists have echoed this, with some coining the term “cartographic colonialism”.

What they said …

“I was alive, and I hadn’t been in a long time.” – Tim Andrews, pig kidney recipient

Tim Andrews was seriously ill with end-stage kidney disease caused by type 2 diabetes and had only a 9% chance of receiving a human kidney within five years, against a more than 40% risk of dying or being removed from the waiting list.

But in a world first, and thanks to a genetically modified kidney from a pig called Wilma, Andrews was kept alive for a record nine months while he waited for a human transplant.

Podcast

Chanel Contos wants to fix our social media algorithms

Consent advocate Chanel Contos is leading a new campaign to push for social media companies to give Australians the choice to “opt in” to the algorithms driving the infinite scroll.

Following her speech at the National Press Club this week, she speaks with political editor Tom McIlroy about why this solution addresses the structural forces influencing misogynistic behaviour – particularly in young men.

Before bed read

Can your boyfriend read? Women are giving their partners the “Illiterate Boyfriend” test on TikTok. Users have compiled a list of what are essentially SAT words for women to ask their male partners to read. Many of these men – this is an overwhelmingly heterosexual activity – fail to finish the list unscathed.

Today’s starter word is: ABLY. You have five goes to get the longest word including the starter word. Play Wordiply.
